Lexington Avenue & East 41st Street, Manhattan

The Low Point

Under one Midtown intersection: an 1852 brick sewer, a 1922 tunnel sewer cut through the schist, water and gas mains, electric duct banks, and a 20-inch steam main, laid in 1924, that dips to fifteen feet below the street to pass beneath Lexington Avenue. On July 18, 2007, water collected at the bottom of that dip, and at 5:56 in the evening the pipe burst.

1

What is under the corner

The street and the soil are taken away, down to the top of the rock. Everything shown is placed from the investigation Con Edison commissioned after the explosion, which mapped the lines under this intersection, and from the city's open data. Pick a system to see it alone, or point at anything to see what it is.

2

Why a steam pipe has a low point

The main carries steam at about 160 psi and 370 °F to buildings along 41st Street. On its way it loses heat through its insulation, and some of the steam turns back into water: about half a pound per foot of pipe per hour. That water, the condensate, runs downhill inside the pipe to the lowest place it can reach. Here that is the dip under Lexington Avenue, where the main drops to cross beneath the other lines.

A 3-inch drain on the pipe's underside, in manhole 6114, carries the condensate up a 2-inch line to two steam traps in manhole 7338. A trap lets water through and closes against steam; these two dumped it into the sewer. Together they could pass 3,700 pounds an hour. The 912 feet of main that drains to this point makes about 400.

3

July 18, 2007

Drag the clock, or play the day. The pool in the pipe and the water around it come from a model of the investigation's numbers: the rain, the water rising in the ground and into the housing, the steam condensing on flooded steel, and what the traps could take away.

    4

    Two things had to go wrong

    Either failure alone would not have done it. With the traps working, the housing would have had to flood almost to the top of the bend before the pool could reach the place that burst. With the housing dry, clogged traps would have taken about a day to let it fill that far. The investigators worked out every pair of trap function and flood level that would fill the pipe to the rupture within the nine hours from 9 AM, without filling it so far that customers on Lexington lost steam. That window is the band below. Pick a pair.

    5

    The hammer

    For hours the pool sat still, and slowly cooled below the temperature of the steam around it. Between about 5:15 and 5:45 PM a control valve about 30 blocks south, CV-3, closed in steps as steam output was cut back to match demand. The pressure on the west side of the intersection rose about 3 psi above the east. That pushed steam down the vertical leg into the cooled water lying in the horizontal pipe. A bubble of steam was trapped in the water and collapsed almost at once, and the water on either side rushed into the space and struck itself.

    A pressure wave goes through water at about 4,000 feet a second, and its size is the Joukowski relation: the water's density, times that speed, times the speed of the impact. The main normally held about 160 psi. To burst it, the pulse had to add at least 1,060. It failed in the File 3 bend on the east side, a bend made to a New York Steam Company drawing in 1924, where the wave had to turn.

    6

    155 years of digging

    Nothing under a Manhattan street is replaced all at once. Each line was laid when it was needed, around whatever was already there, and the old ones stay until they fail. This corner, oldest first:
